Author: tmds

The test I've included fails on Windows.
Something causes the last write time on the extracted directory to be the current time.

It can be a bug in the implementation, though I expect that would also happen on Linux.
It can also be something that is specific to Windows which causes the time to change.
Does someone have an idea on what it might be?

> Something causes the last write time on the extracted directory to be the current time

I didn't look carefully, but I don't see you setting the directory times (Directory.SetLastWriteTime(..)). Without that, the directories are going to have the same time of the last write to a file within them, I think. (Although I thought that was true on Linux, so not sure why it would be only on Windows)

Looks like Directory.SetXx must be used to set a directory timestamp. File.SetXx will not work because Windows requires one extra flag:

https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/e80ef8638b6d3f42add1bb046e032b2eff417473/src/libraries/System.Private.CoreLib/src/System/IO/FileSystem.Windows.cs#L223

While on Unix, it looks like either work, they end up calling utimensat the same way.

> Looks like Directory.SetXx must be used to set a directory timestamp. File.SetXx will not work because Windows requires one extra flag:

Yes, that makes the difference. The tests are passing now on Windows too.
When we close this issue we probably should open an issue for our zip implementation as well as that's also mentioned in that issue

issue_context.title: Directories created by extracting from a tar file do not have timestamps set
issue_context.body:
Related to https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/issues/73825

Extracting a tar file does not set timestamps on the directories it creates. Unix tar do set it.

As an aside, it appears our existing zip implementation doesn't do this either, whereas the zip/unzip tools do set it.

Author: danmoseley
Assignees: -

I made a start at fixing this: https://github.com/danmoseley/runtime/tree/tar.set.directory.time

However, I'm putting it aside because what I see happening (on Windows) is that the directory last written timestamp gets reset to current when a file is written to it. So as it is, the order in which extraction happens will affect the final timestamp. Taking this further would require some inspection of whether `tar` tries to deal with this (eg., by making a second pass through to set timestamps) or has the same problem.

`tar` sets the times on a directory when it finished adding items to it.

For out-of-order archives, a user can manually specify `--delay-directory-restore` which causes `tar` to apply the timestamps when all extraction is done.
Interesting. How important do you believe it is to set the directory timestamps? I guess some users expect the extracted tree to look exactly like the original.

As the gnu man page describes it, it sets the timestamp on each directory when it encounters the first file not in the directory. Does not sound too difficult. Any interest, @tmds 🙂

https://www.gnu.org/software/tar/manual/html_node/Directory-Modification-Times-and-Permissions.html

Yes, you can assign this to me.

> How important do you believe it is to set the directory timestamps? I guess some users expect the extracted tree to look exactly like the original.

I think if this works in .NET 8 that is fine.

From a digital preservation standpoint having the ability to stay as close as possible to the original metadata incl. folder modification times would be ideal, so if a behaviour akin to `tar`'s `--delay-directory-restore` could be provided this would be much appreciated. If there is even a slim chance to move this ahead of the .NET 8 release this would be even better. Thanks for all the great work on tarfile support so far in any case!
@tmds are you still planning on this one? else we can mark up for grabs.
I'll try to make some time for this next week, and if I don't, we can mark it up-for-grabs.

review_comments: @danmoseley the directory last write times get set here.
sorry I wasn't clear -- I meant in the extraction code.

It is calling `TarEntry.AttemptSetLastWriteTime`.

That calls `File.SetLastWriteTime`. Maybe Windows doesn't like this for directories ... :crossed_fingers:
this can probably be replaced with `Path.EndsInDirectorySeparator(..)`
It can't be used for the second caller in this method.

This is copied and changed for directories from:

https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/e80ef8638b6d3f42add1bb046e032b2eff417473/src/libraries/System.Formats.Tar/src/System/Formats/Tar/TarEntry.cs#L552-L562
I might be reading this wrong but isn't `directoryModificationTimes` always empty here with the current implementation? If it's always empty, why even pass it in?

It gets new-ed up by the caller of this method and the same instance is passed to all entries of the archive.
Items get added and removed by the call to `TarHelpers.UpdatePendingModificationTimes` in this method.
